statement: Show that the equation $2^{x}=x^{2}$ has exactly three real roots, and find two of them exactly.
solution: Let $f(x)=2^{x}-x^{2}$. We have $f(2)=0$ and $f(4)=0$, so $x=2$ and $x=4$ are roots. For negative $x$, $f(-1)=\tfrac12-1<0$ and $f(0)=1>0$, so there is a root in $(-1,0)$ (numerically $x\approx-0.7667$). To see there are exactly three, note $f'(x)=2^{x}\ln2-2x$. On $x<0$, $2^{x}\ln2>0$ and $-2x>0$, so $f'(x)>0$: $f$ is strictly increasing and has exactly one negative root. On $x>0$, $f(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to\infty$ and $f$ has at most two more stationary points, giving exactly the two positive roots $2$ and $4$. Thus there are exactly three real roots: $-0.7667\ldots,\;2,\;4$.
hints: Spot the obvious positive roots $x=2$ and $x=4$.
Show $f$ is strictly increasing for $x<0$ to get exactly one negative root.
Argue there can be no further positive roots.
